articles.text: At its most recent meeting, Piedmont City Council heard from Sustainability Program Manager Deniz Ergun about the City’s plans to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in Piedmont. Recently hired to the role, Deniz Ergun has been tasked with helping the City meet ambitious climate goals. During their July 17, 2023 meeting, the City Council approved amendments to their Climate Action Plan 2.0, vowing to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 50% by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality no later than 2045. During her presentation on Monday, February 5, Ergun identified three main items she recommended the City prioritize in 2024 and early 2025 to help meet this goal –developing a building electrification strategy, promoting the adoption of electric vehicles (EV), and increasing community engagement. On developing a building electrification strategy, Ergun suggested a task force to “establish a pathway for the equitable transition of Piedmont’s existing homes and businesses to carbon net zero emissions.” She also explained the importance of this component, as residential buildings accounted for almost half of the greenhouse gas emissions in the City. “The other half are from transportation,” she continued. articles.text: Measure F and the Overall Tax Burden in Piedmont The following letter was sent on January 30 to Piedmont City Council. Editor: The Piedmont league of Women Voters is writing to express concern about Measure F specifically, and more broadly about the piecemeal process for asking Piedmont voters to approve bond measures and special taxes. Our concerns are two-fold. First, while we understand that the City seeks predictable revenue, Measure F’s twelve-year term removes an important means of accountability to voters: the need to seek approval of a special tax on a regular basis. Second, we fear that due to the lack of truly comprehensive long-range planning by the City, Measure F will not be the end of additional special taxes or bond measures through 2037. mont’s taxpayers are currently subject to a sewer tax, a school bond and taxes, a parcel tax, a pool bond, and – in some areas – a utilities undergrounding bond. When the Council approved Measure F for the March 2024 ballot, the Council commented that the $245,000 per year equipment budget in Measure F would not cover all costs for improved City services. The Council even suggested that it might return to voters as soon as November 2024 to request an additional increase in the parcel tax. For many years, it has been known that costly seismic retrofitting is needed for Piedmont’s public safety buildings. The Council has recently contemplated, as part of the housing element, options that could include making improvements to the corporation yard, relocating a sports field, and offering City-funded incentives to developers. These possibilities were not included in the City’s 10-year General Fund financial projections on which the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee based its Measure F recommendation. The league believes that all of the growing needs for City services must be considered as a part of the City’s long-range planning.

articles.text: Editor: Up for discussion at next week’s Planning Commission meeting is the Conditional Use Permit application by Shell Recharge to demolish the old Shell station at 29 Wildwood Avenue and replace it with an Electric Vehicle charging hub. I support the city’s stated goals and commitment regarding EVs and EV infrastructure, and would like to welcome Shell to the neighborhood. However, I firmly oppose their application to establish an unprecedented 24/7 operation at this location. Since the implementation of the CUP process in Piedmont in 1990, no CUP applicant doing business along the Grand Avenue corridor has ever applied for permission to operate before 6 am or after 10 pm. I would venture to say that in the 100 plus years of Piedmont’s incorporation, no business located along this corridor has ever legally done so. The Piedmont Design and Review Guidelines describe the Grand Avenue Commercial District as “fundamentally defined by the surrounding residential buildings and the residential form of Piedmont itself.” The proposed site shares a property line with two private residences. There are four more residences across the street on Wildwood. Many more homes on Wildwood, Fairview, Grand and Olive are within eyesight and/or earshot of the property. These residents are entitled to enjoy the same peace and quiet in the overnight hours that every other Piedmont resident appreciates. To suggest otherwise insults one’s intelligence. In previous Piedmont Post articles announcing the planned charging hub, Jeremy Randolph, Shell Recharge Program Manager, has stated both Shell’s commitment to being a good neighbor and their intention to operate 24/7. These goals are incompatible. A visit to the area in the overnight hours will make it clear to anyone what an unwelcome intrusion 24/7 would be. Hopefully, the Planning Commission and Shell Recharge will make the smart choice and create a win/ win/win situation, compatible with both the city’s and Shell’s goals and with the “residential form of Piedmont itself.” –Don Dare Wildwood Avemue HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY

articles.text: Editor: I am reaching out to convey my concerns regarding the potential consequences of a teachers’ strike, which may inadvertently hinder their pursuit of higher pay rather than support it. While I empathize with teachers advocating for fair compensation, it is crucial to examine the wider repercussions a strike could have on parental support, enrollment, and the overall financial health of our schools. Various factors have been identified as contributors to the current financial challenges our schools are grappling with, such as state funding, community contributions, and enrollment levels. Regrettably, a strike would not tackle the problem of insufficient state funding and could potentially worsen the situation by reducing revenue from both enrollment and community support. The increasing shift of parents moving their children to private schools in our community is evident. It’s also noteworthy that a significant number of parents have openly expressed their consideration of making this transition. I’m concerned a strike could push more parents in that direction, which would lead to significant consequences for vital funding. This would impact enrollment, and we must acknowledge that, whether we prefer it or not, the most substantial donations to our schools often come from individuals who can afford private education. In conclusion, all stakeholders must engage in open dialogue to find alternative solutions that prioritize fair compensation for teachers while also ensuring the financial stability of our schools. A collaborative approach will better serve the interests of our educators, and, most importantly, our students. – Concerned Elementary and Middle School Parent Newsstand copies of the Piedmont Post are available at ­ Mulberry’s Market. The letter said that joining the Coalition means Piedmont educators are “[l]etting outsiders drive APT’s agenda.” In fact, the Coalition arose organically from many years of conversations among East Bay educators, including Piedmont teachers, about the difficulty of surviving here on a typical teacher’s salary, and about how the current teacher shortage is driving schools to a crisis point. All local schools are struggling to attract good teachers as the current generation of veterans retires in increasingly large numbers, while the teacher credentialing programs that should be training a new generation have distressingly (but understandably) low enrollments. Low teacher pay is a systemic problem, and the East Bay Coalition rose out of the desire for a systemic solution. Everyone in the coalition is an actual working educator in the East Bay. Each union that joined the coalition did so freely, in the hope that standing together we’d have a better chance of making positive change. Piedmont educators voted overwhelmingly to join the coalition each year. Common bargaining standards each year were built by group consensus. We recognize meeting the standards is harder for some districts since funding structures differ. But we’ve also watched Piedmont slip lower in comparison to other local districts in compensation over the past few years. Last year’s 7.5% increase was among the lowest in the Coalition, and unlike several other local districts, we received no increase in district contributions to health care premiums. For this year, given inflation and a dramatic spike in Kaiser costs, an 8.22% salary increase is actually the minimum needed to avoid an effective compensation cut. That’s why we stood firm by the Coalition bargaining standards to the point of going to impasse. And we’ve watched as many surrounding districts have indeed settled their contracts at or above the 8.22% COLA. Others have gone to impasse with offers much higher than PUSD’s current offer. Now that we’re in mediation, we’re no longer obligated to hold to the Coalition standards, much as we believe they are good ones. articles.text: Barbara Lee (D), U.S. Representative for California’s 12th Congressional District (which encompasses Piedmont, Oakland, and most of Northern Alameda County) is running for the U.S. Senate seat formerly occupied by the late Senator Diane Feinstein. As a leading candidate, along with Adam Schiff (D), Katie Porter (D), and Steve Garvey (R), Lee’s run for senate has added fire to the already exciting race since she announced her candidacy in February 2023. Her candidacy has also raised questions about who will take Lee’s her long-held seat in the House of Representatives. “Senator Feinstein was a friend, a mentor, and a role model who, from being the first woman elected as mayor of San Francisco to being the first woman to represent California in the U.S. Senate, broke many glass ceilings for others behind her,” said Lee. “It’s time to keep breaking glass ceilings. I’m running to be California’s Senator, and only the fourth Black woman ever to serve in the Senate, because I am a consistent progressive who has never backed down to fight for working people – whether it’s affordable, accessible health care, climate justice or an economy that works for everyone.” Lee also called on the residents of Piedmont to go to the polls on election day. “I am committed to the unfinished work of advancing equality for all and would be honored to have the people of Piedmont’s support to be their representative U.S. Senate candidate Barbara Lee in the U.S. Senate,” said Lee. Lee was elected to Congress in 1998. Her bid for a seat in the Senate has raised questions of who her successor in the House of Representatives will be. articles.text: The arrival of the Year of the Dragon will be celebrated by the Piedmont Asian American Club at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens School this Friday, February 9 from 5:30-7:30 p.m. Around 80 student and adult volunteers from PAAC will host the Lunar New Year event highlighted by performances, crafts, a lion dance and dim sum. With the exception of calligraphy, all the craft and game tables will be new this year. Attendees will delight in making a dragon puppet, a lucky mandarin, paper fan and a spin drum. “Growing up in Asia, Lunar New Year is a festive and important holiday. articles.text: As part of this year’s International Holocaust Remembrance Day on January 27, approximately 200 San Francisco East Bay Jewish community members came together to honor and remember victims of the Shoah and spread the urgent message: “Never Again Is Now”, linking the responsibility to never forget with the urgent need to remain vigilant against the current rising tide of antisemitism. With a generous sponsorship from Eileen Ruby, president of the Jewish Community Federation of the Bay Area, organizers from the Jewish Community of Piedmont, including Donna Friedman Meir, Nicki Gilbert, Sari Kaplan, Melanie Marcus, Lili Naveh, and Sharon Sagiv, developed a moving program with local Jewish community leaders, bringing a focus on Holocaust survivors, the atrocities of October 7 in Israel, and recent local antisemitic attacks. The event began at the gates of the Home of Eternity Jewish Cemetery in Oakland, where many survivors are laid to rest. Aliza Grayevsky Somekh, the visionary behind this event and owner of Israeli-owned catering company Bishulum San Francisco, opened the ceremony and Rabbi Mark Bloom of Temple Beth Abraham led the attendees in prayers. “International Holocaust Remembrance Day is our day not only to remember, it is our day to remind the whole world how fast things can go tragically wrong. It is time to act and bring our community together,” said Grayevsky Somekh. Participants shared stories with each other as they walked in a candlelight vigil along Piedmont Avenue to Pomella, an Israeli-owned and operated restaurant. “It is our privilege to provide respite and comfort to our community,” said Mica Talmor, chef and owner of Pomella, which has become an impromptu meeting place for Jewish community members since October 7, and has also endured antisemitic attacks and a loss of business. Rabbi Bloom, NCSY Youth Director Tani Polansky, and Beth Jacob Congregation Rabbi Gershon Albert of Oakland led a musical havdalah service, after which Holocaust survivors, Sanne DeWitt, 89, and Magda Silberman, 95, shared their experiences as young people during the Holocaust. At the age of four, Ms. DeWitt was smuggled from Germany to Holland, and then traveled by ferry to England, eventually ending up in the south of Wales. “Courage is in the DNA of the Jewish people,” she said. “Just as we rose after the Holocaust, we will rise again.” Ms. Silberman survived the Auschwitz and Ravensbrook concentration camps, work camps and munition factories in Germany. As a young and able person, she was forced to sort through the belongings of murdered Jews, and had access to shoes, clothes and food, which kept her alive through death marches, starvation and horrendous conditions. Ms. Silberman reminded attendees to “never give up hope, value family and good friends, and keep the story of the survivors alive. The second and third generation must continue the work of telling the stories of survivors.” Additional speakers included Yoav Harlev, the organizer of the group of volunteers who stand in daily vigil on the Highway 24 overpass in Lafayette with posters demanding the release of the hostages, and Dorit Dorenz, a victim of a recent antisemitic attack in nearby El Cerrito. “In unity there is strength,” said Dorenz as she courageously encouraged the crowd to work together to stand up against antisemitism. Harlev, who grew up on Kibbutz Kissufim along the border with Gaza and Israel, is connected to at least 105 of 136 hostages still in captivity. “I’m shattered and hurting inside. It is my calling to make sure that we don’t lose sight of these innocent hostages that are there, suffering every day,” he said. Event organizer Donna Friedman Meir reminded all those present that, “Never Again is Now. It means that in this moment we must stand together, we must show up for each other in whatever ways we can: support local Jewish and Israeli businesses, show up when advocacy is needed, be good neighbors, check in with one another, and educate the next generation.” The event ended on a note of hope with a heartfelt rendition of “One Day” by Matisyahu, and Israel’s national anthem, “Hatikvah” – literally “The Hope.”
articles.title: Piedmont Jewish families honor International Holocaust Remembrance Day

articles.text: Girl Scouts in Troop 33943: Sai Ahuja, Elizabeth Ackerman, Zayda Weber, Emma Syhabout, Imogen Weber, Shaan Ahuja, Josie & Georgie. Not pictured: Sicheng Wu and Olivia Chan. On Saturday, January 27, Piedmont Middle School 7th grade Girl Scouts in Troop 33943 gathered to work on posters, donation bins and paint a donation stand for their 2024 Service Project, a Period Product Drive. “We are doing the drive to help people who have periods to have better access to period products for their physical and mental health. We are doing this drive to help eliminate period poverty,” explained Zayda Weber. Troop 33943 also partnered with Lola Biehn, president of the Flow Club at Piedmont High School, who also works to improve community access to sustainable period products. From February 1 to March 10 Girls Scouts in Troop 33943 will be collecting new, unopened packages of tampons. menstrual pads, period underwear, and menstrual cups. Please donate new, unopened period products into collection bins located at: • Mulberry’s Market • Donation Stand at the corner of Oakland and Grand Ave • Beach Elementary • Havens Elementary • Piedmont Middle School • Millennium High School • Piedmont High School Troop 33943 has partnered with Oakland Elizabeth House, a residence for women with children, and Alameda County Food Bank to distribute the donated products to the community. Dr. Amy Vallerie, a Troop Leader and the Regional Lead for Pediatric and Adolescent Gynecology at Kaser Oakland noted, “Periods are the number one loss of productivity for school and work for women of a reproductive age. And adding stigma, embarrassment and inability to access appropriate menstrual products, in addition to pain, heavy menstrual cycles, sometimes period related migraines - Is just adding more and more barriers towards young women achieving their full potential.” “We do this drive because many people cannot afford period products,” explained Sicheng Wu. “This drive helps these people get their needs met, which improves their health. I’m proud to be part of it.”
articles.title: Girl Scouts launch donation drive for period products

articles.text: Love is in the air – it’s February. It’s easy to think that the opportunity for creativity around Valentine’s Day is in crafting cards, making homemade Valentines cookies or planning the ultimate date night. But, what if the actual act of creativity for Valentine’s Day is the process of creating relationships themselves? Building a relationship of any kind–marriage, significant other, friendship, parent/child–is a creative process because it requires constant growth, curiosity and openness to possibility to continuously nourish and deepen the connection between people. When you meet someone new, you have to be open to getting to know them, you have to take a risk to put yourself out there to possibly be rejected and you have to get deeply curious about the other person. Openness, risk-taking and curiosity are three core traits of creativity. Fun fact: A recent study from Northwestern University found that people who have a creative mindset find their life partners more desirable and attractive longer than those who do not regularly practice creativity. Huh? How does creativity connect to finding your hubby or wife attractive? Well, creative people are willing to play with each other, try new things and reinvent to keep things new and fresh. And let’s face it, if you are in a marriage and you have children, it is easy to get stuck in a romantic rut. So a willingness to get creative helps avoid just being in the same routine day in and day out. We don’t often give ourselves credit for the creativity it requires to get to know a new person and then to maintain intimacy through a whole series of different types of challenges. Even in friendships we are in constant problem-solving mode, which is a form of creativity. We have busy lives and we need to figure out how to find time to hang out or we might not have the same hobbies or interests and have to find common ground. For this Valentine’s Day, take a moment to notice how you have brought creativity to the relationships that means the most to you: • Have you expressed appreciation in a fun or novel way? • Have you created intimacy through vulnerability and revealing your emotions? • Have you found opportunities for play and laughter? • Have you made plans that bring people together to form meaningful connections? • Have you overcome obstacles and deepened bonds? I’m proud to be part of it.” Thinking Outside the Classroom Love is the ultimate creative act By Nina Meehan Love is in the air – it’s February. It’s easy to think that the opportunity for creativity around Valentine’s Day is in crafting cards, making homemade Valentines cookies or planning the ultimate date night. But, what if the actual act of creativity for Valentine’s Day is the process of creating relationships themselves? Building a relationship of any kind–marriage, significant other, friendship, parent/child–is a creative process because it requires constant growth, curiosity and openness to possibility to continuously nourish and deepen the connection between people. When you meet someone new, you have to be open to getting to know them, you have to take a risk to put yourself out there to possibly be rejected and you have to get deeply curious about the other person. Openness, risk-taking and curiosity are three core traits of creativity. Fun fact: A recent study from Northwestern University found that people who have a creative mindset find their life partners more desirable and attractive longer than those who do not regularly practice creativity. Huh? How does creativity connect to finding your hubby or wife attractive? Well, creative people are willing to play with each other, try new things and reinvent to keep things new and fresh. And let’s face it, if you are in a marriage and you have children, it is easy to get stuck in a romantic rut. So a willingness to get creative helps avoid just being in the same routine day in and day out. We don’t often give ourselves credit for the creativity it requires to get to know a new person and then to maintain intimacy through a whole series of different types of challenges. Even in friendships we are in constant problem-solving mode, which is a form of creativity. We have busy lives and we need to figure out how to find time to hang out or we might not have the same hobbies or interests and have to find common ground. For this Valentine’s Day, take a moment to notice how you have brought creativity to the relationships that means the most to you: • Have you expressed appreciation in a fun or novel way? • Have you created intimacy through vulnerability and revealing your emotions? • Have you found opportunities for play and laughter? • Have you made plans that bring people together to form meaningful connections? • Have you overcome obstacles and deepened bonds? Why not celebrate love and creativity all at once pm February 14 and long after? articles.text: Last autumn, I traveled to Maui with my family. It was my first time in Hawaii, and I was more than excited to experience the beauty of the island. I had one goal in mind: to enjoy their traditional shaved ice. Due to the fires, we stayed on the South side of the island. However, on October 8th, the West side was ‘reopened’. Eager to see the other side of the island we climbed into our rental car and We were struck with horror when we saw the ruins. Blackened trees dotted the parched landscape, and buildings stood half supported. Destruction was everywhere, whispered in the air, through the time that seemed to stand still, in the sickening feeling of sadness that touched all of us. Disheartened, we headed back to our condo. As we traveled through the mountains, we spotted a shaved ice sign, and, with the motivation of treating ourselves to the iconic Hawaiian dessert, we pulled into Lorraine Shaved ice, where we were greeted by a kind and welcoming couple. Like many small, owner-run businesses on Maui, Lorraine Shave Ice in Kahakuloa has suffered due to the lack of tourists who avoided visiting the island as an effect of the deadly fires. Also like many small, owner-run businesses on Maui they all care deeply about the island and the people who come to experience the beauty. To see the destruction and negative impact on these humble businesses is truly heart wrenching. There has been a lot of controversy surrounding the reopening, with people arguing that the island needs time to heal, others claiming that tourism could be beneficial to the island as one of its main revenue streams. I’m not going to say if one party is wrong, but I will say what needs to be said: Maui needs to heal. While one side argues that Maui needs the isolation to repair and rejuvenate, the other believes that tourism will aid them, especially in the economical sense. However, the strain that the fire has pushed upon the island and its inhabitants is a pain no one person can imagine. So much rich history and culture, destroyed. As the new year dawns on us, we focus on healing and improving ourselves for the coming year. With the giving spirit and hope for renewal, the new year is that perfect time to help this beautiful island to revive itself. Daisy Seymour is an eighth grader at Piedmont Middle School. Lorraine Shaved Ice, a family-owned business in the mountains of Hawaii was heavily impacted by the loss of tourists after the devastating fires on Maui in August 2023.

articles.text: The 55th Annual Leonard Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest will officially use the artwork of PHS senior Kira Pan as the poster for the event. The famed competition, founded by PHS science teacher Leonard J. Waxdeck, will use the theme “A Rose By Any Other Name Would Sound As Sweet,” which coordinates with the artwork. Pan’s poster will be used in all publicity for the event including the cover for the program. For her effort, Pan will receive a large framed copy of the poster, two tickets to the show and a $200 prize. “I’ve always loved the annual Bird Calling Contest at Piedmont and am excited to contribute to the tradition,” said Pan. PHS Librarian Kathryn Levenson will serve as Chair of the Bird Calling Contest Committee, her final year at the school. “In the early days of the Bird Calling Contest, our posters were commissioned from professional artists. In more modern times, we have turned to the amazing talent of our Piedmont High School artists,” stated Levenson. Pan served as the graphics editor of The Piedmont Highlander (TPH) last year, where she honed skills as a digital artist. She is currently the co-editor-in-chief of TPH and continues to contribute art for the school publication. “My inspiration for the piece was the bluebird because I love their bright colors and how they’re believed to symbolize good luck. Working in TPH has taught me how to integrate design elements cohesively, so I decided to incorporate the rose theme into the microphone drawing and have the bluebirds hold up the banner,” explained Pan. The theme “A Rose By Any Other Name Would Sound As Sweet” is taken from William Shakespeare’s play Romeo and Juliet. The bird calling acts are composed of groups of students performing for local celebrity judges. Acts are scored on authenticity of call, information about the bird provided by the students, poise of delivery, creativity and artistry. For decades, the winning Piedmont bird callers would appear and perform on the Johnny Carson Show and later on the David Letterman Show. The Bird Calling Contest will take place on Friday, March 29, at 7:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater at Piedmont High School. Tickets, which go on sale on March 1, are $25 for general admission and $15 for students. PHS senior Kira Pan’s winning poster design. ®

articles.text: Seven fifth graders – Nicholas Phung Theodore Gottscalk, Nicholas Phung, Maxwell Howng, Brendan Edesses, Andrew Lee, Madison Kao, and Julian Huang – made a presentation about the Lunar New Year at Wildwood Elementary School. Theodore and his mom, Stefanie Wong, have been doing this presentation since he was in kindergarten. This year, he switched it up and invited his friends to present with him. He does this presentation every year to spread awareness and acceptance of the Chinese culture. Stefanie started presenting when Theo was six. This was because she experienced racism when she moved to a new school in Canada where she and her sister were the only Asian kids in the school. As a result, Stefanie wanted to teach children about her culture and ethnicity. She does this Theo Gottschalk teaches his classmates how to say “Happy New Year” in Chinese. Photos by Carolyn Pan Madison Fishman has a question for her classmate Maxwell Howng as Nikias Moulatsios, Ms. Tang, Max Centeno, and James Wilson look on. at Lunar New Year and Mid Autumn Festival presentations at Wildwood. In Nicholas’s part of the presentation, he talked about why the first day of the Lunar New Year moves around in the Chinese calendar. Then Maxwell informed the crowd about some traditions for Lunar New Year. After that, Brendan told the class how certain foods can have different meanings. Finally, Madison described some taboos that are important during the Lunar New Year. Following that Theo taught his peers some things to say in Mandarin like “ni hao”. And finally they ended the presentation with Julian naming what animals in the coming years will be. Now in their last year at Wildwood School, they hope that another family or group will continue this tradition every year in the coming years. The trip was a joint effort between the Core teachers and the Science teachers, which aimed to provide an experiential aspect to concepts learned in both Social Studies and Science this school year. The group of approximately 180 students, 50 parent volunteers, and seven teachers visited seven “stations” with various learning goals. The African Hall’s special exhibit, the Human Odyssey, took students through the evolution of early humans, reinforcing the very first unit of study from their social studies class last August. Students noted the special structures of cnidarians such as jellyfish and anemones in the aquarium. Echinoderms such as sea cucumbers and urchins, Mollusks such as scallops and octopus, and Arthropods such as crab and shrimp as well as all of these animals’ interactions with one another in their environment. In a reptile hunt that took students all over the museum from the aquarium to the swamp to the rainforest, the focus was on the various adaptations the reptiles have to live in a variety of environments. There were two special exhibits on display, Hidden Wonders and Color of Life. In Hidden Wonders, there were collections of various animals, plants and fossils from around the world. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. articles.text: The Highlanders wrapped up a productive week with two wins to create a three-game winning streak. They defeated St. Joseph in Alameda 67-55 on Monday, February 5 and dominated Alameda 58-39 at Binks Rawlings Gym on Wednesday, January 31. PHS now holds a 15-9 record going into its final two games of the season. “We try to go one game at a time, but I knew St. Joe would be one of our toughest games. It was our third game against them and when you play anyone that many times, it’s going to be tough,” said coach Ben Spencer. “They were playing for their playoff lives.” Piedmont will travel to San Leandro tonight, February 7, and host Castro Valley two days later, when the team will honor its six seniors on the roster: Brit Burden, Arjun Bornstein, Finn Burke, Thorin Holmes, Declan Linnane, and transfer student Scott Cooley. With two wins, PHS could set itself up nicely for a high seeding in the Division 3 North Coast Section playoffs. “Right now, we can more consistent with our energy levels on the defensive end. We just need to lock in defensively, trusting each other, and play for each other,” said Burden. “We have to get ready for NCS, and these games are preparing us for that. It’s good to get some wins and get on a roll going into NCS,” said junior guard Ravi Silverberg. Burden had a strong 23-point performance in Monday’s win over St. Joseph, building stronger into the second half as he adjusted against the Pilots’ tall forward Gabriel Enyinwa. “Gabe’s a great player. I’ve been matching up against him since freshman year and it’s always fun to go against him. Those type of players just push me and make me better,” said Burden. Against the Hornets, everything was falling into place for Silverberg, who led scoring with 18 points. “The drive was there the whole game, so I just kept attacking. I didn’t feel like anyone could guard me, so I just kept attacking. I got to the rim a lot and the points added up,” said Silverberg. 67-55 over St. Joseph Piedmont led 14-13 by the end of the first quarter and 27-25 at halftime. With a big 22-point third quarter, Piedmont created some breathing room at 49-37, and added 18 more points in the final going. There were four lead changes in the third quarter until Dillon Casey put PHS up 33-31 after drawing a foul on a layup. It was the start of an 11-0 scoring run to put the Highlanders ahead 41-31. The Pilots battled in the fourth to narrow the deficit to one possession at 53-51, but from there Piedmont scored 12 unanswered points to jump ahead 65-51 in the late minutes. Final stats: Burden had 23 points, Linnane had 13 points, Casey scored 11, Silverberg had 10, Bornstein scored six, while PJ Brayer and Thorin Holmes has two. articles.text: When mentioning the athletic accomplishments of student-athletes at Piedmont High, it can be easy to lose track of those who have continued their careers in college. In this week’s issue, we take a look at Ana Romanczuk of track and field, Kai Johnson of basketball, and Gavin Horne of track and field. Photo courtesy of Morgan State Athletics Kai Johnson, PHS Class of 2021, is a junior on Morgan State’s basketball team. As a freshman, she played in 26 games and had 19 points, 14 steals, 16 rebounds, three assists, and one block. For Piedmont, she was a team captain her final two years. She was a major part of a strong four-year run for the girls’ basketball team, finishing with records of 23-7 in 2018, 20-11 in 2019, 21-7 in 2020, and 15-3 in 2021’s shortened pandemic season. Romancuzk primarily competed in shot, discus, and pole vault in high school. She reached the NCS Bayshore Championship in the discus, where she was 19th with a distance of 66 feet, 3 inches. articles.text: Piedmont Fencing Team is halfway through its season and quickly approaching the prestigious Junior Olympics in Charlotte, North Carolina on February 16-19. Piedmont High juniors Teresa McKay and Oliver Greenebaum have already qualified for the tournament, and former Piedmont resident Sophie Choi is also hitting high levels for the club which trains at the community church. “Teresa, Oliver and Sophie all qualified for Junior Olympics and also qualified for Nationals in the summer. We’re about mid-way through our schedule and we’re doing really well,” said veteran coach David Sinkkonen. Since the Post covered the Piedmont Fencing Team in July last year following the National Championship in Phoenix, several of the club’s top fencers have progressed tremendously. McKay has earned two Bronze medals for third place finishes thus far, improving her win ratio in overall matches from 19 percent last year to 42 percent currently. “Teresa has been putting up great numbers. In fencing, you lose more than you win. It’s kind of like the baseball batting average, so for her to have that high of a percentage says a lot. She’s awesome,” said Sinkkonen. McKay has 34 wins so far this season. She finished third at the Air Force ROC in Colorado Springs on October 1 in the Division 2 women’s foil ladder and was third of 11 at the Wasatch Fencing RYC/ RJCC on September 23 in Utah in the junior women’s ladder. She recently competed in the women’s Division 1-A at the Battle of the Bay in San Jose. She will compete in the junior and cadet women’s categories at the Junior Olympics. Sophie Kim (left) and Teresa McKay will be representing Piedmont Fencing Team at the Junior Olympics. Oliver Greenebaum (left), a junior at Piedmont High School, has qualified for the Junior Olympics. “Teresa has had an excellent season and has increased her rating to E and D all in one weekend [at the Air Force ROC]. She was able to qualify for Junior Olympics, which is awesome. There are college recruiters looking at her,” said Sinkkonen on Teresa’s development. Greenebaum has also earned two Bronze medals in 2023/2024, putting together a win ratio of 36.3 percent with 41 wins. His ratio has improved by seven percent over the last year. On January 1, he competed in the Hangover Open in Denver, where he increased his rating. “He’s doing pretty darn well. He had a tournament in Denver and earned his D rating and also qualified for Junior Olympics,” said Sinkkonen.

articles.text: On view through October 17, Into View: New Voices, New Stories is an exhibition of recent acquisitions by the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco that disrupts the dominant narratives of contemporary art by bringing the fantasies, joys, sorrows and yearnings of Asian American and Asian diaspora artists into vibrant dialogue with one another to challenge common conceptions of Asian art history. Through paintings, sculptures, ceramics, prints, video, and mixed-media works, this unique presentation places different time periods, genres, and political and social concerns into one exhibit, reimagining art world conventions to reflect this group of primarily women and LGBTQ Asian artists. Many of the included works are from artists from the Bay Area or with ties to the region. Throughout the exhibition, works from prominent local voices join past and present via a reclamation of traditional imagery. For instance, Heroine by Rupy C. Tut (b. India, 1985) — a painted reimagining of a scene from Punjabi folklore — and Nuwa’s Hands by Cathy Lu (b. United States, 1984) — a contemporary envisioning of a Chinese mother goddess, rendered in a dangling complex of ceramic forms — mingle interrogations of utopian ideals, the experience of migration, and what it means to be a woman protagonist. Fresh approaches to well-established genres also boldly defy expectations. What appears to be a traditional Chinese landscape painting by Wu Chi-Tsung (b. Taiwan, 1981) is in fact formed from sculptural layers of crumpled photosensitive paper, while an experimental film by TT Takemoto (b. United States, 1967) peers beneath the surface of documentary footage of Japanese American women factory workers to reveal an intimate social atmosphere. “At a moment of heightened turmoil domestically and around the globe, Into View feels so needed right now, entwining concepts like mythology, cosmology, political uprisings, social intimacy and ecology as viable alternatives to our current systems and empowering audiences to rethink possibilities in their own lives,” said Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art & Programs Naz Cuguoglu. The Asian Art Museum (200 Larkin St.) is open Thursdays from 1 p.m. to 8 p.m., and Fridays through Mondays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tickets ($20 general, $17 ages 65 and up, $13 ages 13 to 17 and college students) are available at asianart.org. articles.text: Lee Mingwei: Rituals of Care, the Taiwanese American artist’s first survey exhibition in the U.S., will open at the de Young Museum in San Francisco on Saturday, February 17, to run through July 7. The show features seven projects made between 1995 and 2024 that place visitors at the center of interactive acts of generosity and care, asking how art can be a conduit for social connection and healing. Mingwei spent his formative years in San Francisco. Inspired by personal experiences of loss and resilience and major world events such as 9/11, the Iraq War and the COVID-19 pandemic, Mingwei (b. 1964) has, over the course of his career, created participatory mixed-media installations and performances that transform ordinary gestures like writing, sweeping, mending, or breathing into rituals of engagement and solace. The Letter Writing Project (1998–present) draws from the human need to communicate thoughts and feelings left unsaid, keenly felt by the artist after the death of his maternal grandmother. Consisting of three writing booths and an accessible writing station, the latter project invites visitors to write the letter they have always meant to send but never have, and to decide whether to address their letters and have the museum post them, or leave the letters unsealed for others to read. In The Mending Project (2009–present), Lee Mingwei transforms the simple act of sewing into an opportunity to connect. Visitors are invited to bring items of clothing that need mending to the installation, which consists of a table, two chairs, and a wall of colorful, cone-shaped spools of thread. The show features seven projects made between 1995 and 2024 that place visitors at the center of interactive acts of generosity and care, asking how art can be a conduit for social connection and healing. Mingwei spent his formative years in San Francisco. Inspired by personal experiences of loss and resilience and major world events such as 9/11, the Iraq War and the COVID-19 pandemic, Mingwei (b. 1964) has, over the course of his career, created participatory mixed-media installations and performances that transform ordinary gestures like writing, sweeping, mending, or breathing into rituals of engagement and solace. Into View at Asian Art Museum By Selen Ozturk On view through October 17, Into View: New Voices, New Stories is an exhibition of recent acquisitions by the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco that disrupts the dominant narratives of contemporary art by bringing the fantasies, joys, sorrows and yearnings of Asian American and Asian diaspora artists into vibrant dialogue with one another to challenge common conceptions of Asian art history. Through paintings, sculptures, ceramics, prints, video, and mixed-media works, this unique presentation places different time periods, genres, and political and social concerns into one exhibit, reimagining art world conventions to reflect this group of primarily women and LGBTQ Asian artists. Many of the included works are from artists from the Bay Area or with ties to the region. Throughout the exhibition, works from prominent local voices join past and present via a reclamation of traditional imagery. For instance, Heroine by Rupy C. Tut (b. India, 1985) — a painted reimagining of a scene from Punjabi folklore — and Nuwa’s Hands by Cathy Lu (b. articles.text: Nora: A Doll’s House, Scottish playwright Stef Smith’s innovative take on Henrik Ibsen’s classic play, is being performed at City Lights Theatre in San Jose through Sunday, February 18. It’s 1918. And 1968. And 2018. Nora: A Doll’s House, Scottish playwright Stef Smith’s innovative take on the Ibsen classic, sets the action in three decades in a show being performed at City Lights Theatre in San Jose through Sunday, February 18. Nora plays the part in the play of the flawless wife and mother. But she has a secret that threatens to upend her seemingly perfect existence. Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen challenged social norms and outraged audiences when his work A Doll’s House debuted on-stage in 1879. Smith’s new iteration of the play looks back at the roles that women have played during the fight for female suffrage, the swinging sixties, and the modern day, and wonders how far we’ve really come. In an interview with The Standard (U.K.), Smith said she chose the years 1918, 1968 and 2018 because they represent important chapters in women’s history: the first time women were allowed to vote in Britain, legal acknowledgement of reproductive rights in Britain and the aftermath of the #MeToo movement. Three actresses alternate playing Nora and her closest friend, Christine, but Nora’s husband Thomas is always portrayed by the same man. “It’s like the men are in stasis, they find themselves trapped in time, whereas the women have to be more malleable and change with the times,” Smith said. Nora: A Doll’s House premiered in 2019 at Citizens Theatre in Glasgow, followed by an acclaimed production at the Young Vic Theatre in London. Raves have included “beautiful and explosively significant” (The Scotsman), “an explosive couple of hours” (The Herald) and “a radical, stunning reworking of the play” (British Theatre). Smith calls her work “predominantly political, seeking to unearth unheard stories.” Her other plays include Girl in the Machine, Enough, and Human Animals. Smith also writes for the screen, with credits including the BBC Scotland coming-of-age drama Float. Director Angie Higgins is making her City Lights directing debut but is a career veteran, having helmed shows at Limelight Theater, Utopia Theatre Project, Broadway West, Northside Theatre Company, Santa Clara Players and Silicon Valley Shakespeare, where she has been Artistic Director for the past 10 seasons. Tickets ($28-$67) for the play at City Lights Theater (529 S. Second St.) are available at cltc. org, or through the box office at 408-295-4200.

articles.text: Cal Performances at UC Berkeley will present a special double-billed program of The Rite of Spring by choreographer Pina Bausch and a new companion piece, common ground[s] by Germaine Acogny and Malou Airaudo. The production will premiere on Friday, February 16 at 8 p.m., with performances on Saturday and Sunday, February 17-18. This will be the first-ever performance of Bausch’s Rite of Spring choreography in the Bay Area, a piece widely regarded as one of the most influential dance works of the 20th century. “This is the first time that [The Rite of Spring] is done not with an existing company, but with dancers who came together specifically for this piece,” explained Salomon Bausch, Pina Bausch’s son and the Executive Director of the Pina Bausch Foundation. The Rite of Spring will feature 30 dancers from 14 African countries, all assembled through a collaboration between Germany’s Pina Bausch Foundation, Senegal’s École des Sables, and the UK’s Sadler’s Wells Ballet Company. “I’m very excited to see the impact of their personalities and their diverse dance backgrounds on the piece but also vice versa; how the piece influences the dancers, both as artists and as human beings,” said Bausch. “I’ve always felt that this was an African dance,” said dancer Germaine Acogny, “The rituals are the same. And that music has an extraordinary pagan, terrestrial power. I even wonder whether Stravinsky was possessed when he composed it.” The Rite of Spring first premiered in 1913 in Paris, performed by the acclaimed Ballet Russes. In a controversial decision, a relatively-unknown Igor Stravinsky decided to base the composition and ballet on traditional Russian pagan rituals and folk dances, causing a near-riot on opening night. A moderated post-performance discussion will take place on Friday, February 16, and post-performance community conversations will be held on Saturday and Sunday, February 17 and 18. Tickets are $38–$86. Tickets for all performances are available at calperformances.org, by phone at 642-9988, and in person at the Ticket Office at Zellerbach Hall, Tuesday–Friday, 12–5:30 p.m. and Saturday–Sunday, 1–5 p.m. Germaine Acogny (back) and Malou Airaudo pose for a promotional photo for their new companion piece, common ground[s].

articles.text: For more than two decades, Kitka Women’s Vocal Ensemble’s annual Wintersongs concerts have explored songs from across Eastern Europe that summon the return of light and hope in times of difficulty and darkness. On Friday, February 9 and Saturday, February 10 at 8 p.m. the ensemble will perform Wintersongs in Candlelight at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland. Featuring seasonal songs from Balkan, Baltic, Caucasian, Mediterranean, and Slavic lands, Wintersongs highlights include music expressing gratitude and wonder for the miracle of creation; folk carols that bestow blessings upon family and friends gathered around hearth fires and feast tables; hymns of faith and devotion to divine beings; humorous songs that heal with laughter; songs that summon hope for rebirth and renewal; and choral callings for peace on Earth. Kitka is an American women’s vocal arts ensemble inspired by traditional songs and vocal techniques from Eastern Europe and Eurasia. Founded in 1979 as an offshoot of the Westwind International Folk Ensemble, Kitka began as a grassroots group of amateur singers from diverse ethnic and musical backgrounds who shared a passion for the stunning dissonances, asymmetric rhythms, intricate ornamentation, and resonant strength of traditional Eastern European women’s vocal music. For four decades, the ninewoman Oakland ensemble has developed a vast, breathtaking repertoire of traditional songs from the Balkans, Caucasus and Slavic lands, as well as new material composed for the group drawing on those traditional vocal practices. Traveling to rural communities in Armenia and Bulgaria, Ukraine and Georgia, Serbia and Turkey, they’ve gathered songs and communed with elders who are often the last links to centuries-old traditions. A frequently occurring symbolic word in Balkan folk songs, “Kitka” means bouquet in Bulgarian and Macedonian. Tickets are $25-$50 at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church, 114 Montecito Avenue (near Lake Merritt) are available at stpaulsoakland.org/concerts. The Kitka Women’s Vocal Ensemble will perform at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland on Friday and Saturday, February 9-10.

articles.text: Four East Bay artists will showcase their work at Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue, Piedmont. The exhibition, titled Moments that Give Pause, will be open for viewing on Saturdays and Sundays, February 17 to March 3, from noon to 3 pm, with an opening reception on February 17 from 6 pm to 9 pm. These artists use divergent materials – painting, fiber, and cut paper – but share a common theme of celebration in the moment. Their exhibition is an invitation to pause from the intensity of life and to contemplate beauty. Featured Artists Carol Aust is a figurative painter based in Oakland. Her acrylic paintings depict people on journeys through emotional landscapes. Her work can be viewed at www.carolaust.com. Debra Collins creates delicate and intricate hand cut paper works of “internal meanderings.” Her work can be viewed at www. debraacollins.com. Carol Aust, “Mother and Child #49,” acrylics on panel, 16”x20” Gretchen McCondochie, “Embroidered Bird,” embroidery thread, 3”x3” Leslie Crisfield explores the contrast of light and dark and “wow moments” that stop her in her tracks. Her acrylic paintings can be viewed at www.lesliecrisfield.artcall.org. Gretchen McCondochie creates mixed media pieces, textiles, drawings and paintings that reflect her need for nature and stillness. Her work can be viewed at www.instagram.com/gretchendailydrawing. At the opening reception, live music of jazz standards will be provided by the Backyard Trio, with Chris Cooper on guitar, Jessie Ortiz on piano, and Baird Wheatley on saxophone. For more information, contact Carol Aust at carol.aust.art@ gmail.com .

articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony will celebrate the Lunar New Year with their Year of the Dragon concert and banquet with 4 p.m. pre-concert festivities, a 5 p.m. performance and a 6:30 p.m. post-concert feast on Saturday, February 17 at Davies Symphony Hall. Lunar New Year is the most important holiday for many cultures in East, South and Southeast Asia, and is celebrated by people of Asian descent worldwide. This year’s celebration marks the 24th anniversary of the SF Symphony’s signature event, an elegant celebration of the Lunar New Year drawing upon vibrant Asian traditions past and present. The celebration begins at 4 p.m. with pre-concert lobby festivities open to all ticket holders, featuring an array of entertainment and activities including dragon dancers, fortune readers, calligraphy artists, and cultural performances. Conductor Mei-Ann Chen and the orchestra will then open the concert with Li Huan-Zhi’s energetic Spring Festival Overture and Phoon Yew Tien’s joyful New Year Greetings. The orchestra will then perform Jasmine Flower, a folk song from China’s Jiangsu province, which was arranged for orchestra by Li Wenping in 1999. The program continues with Flower Drum Song from Feng Yang and Girl from Da Ban City from Huang Ruo’s Folk Songs for Orchestra, originally commissioned and performed by the San Francisco Symphony at their 2012 Chinese New Year concert. Also on the program is Vivian Fung’s Pizzicato, which features sounds inspired by two Chinese instruments — the pipa and qin — as well as Indonesian gamelan music. Violinist Paul Huang will join the Symphony to play music from Tan Dun’s violin concerto, Fire Ritual, originally written for and premiered by violinist Eldbjørg Hemsing. Concluding the program are Che Chang’s Ali Mountain Evergreen, a piece that evokes the staggering scale of Ali Mountain in Taiwan, and Chen Ge Xin’s Gong Xi Gong Xi, a popular Chinese Lunar New Year song that translates to “Congratulations” or “Wishing You Happiness and Prosperity.” The post-concert Lunar New Year Banquet begins at 6:30 p.m. in Zellerbach Rehearsal Hall, located at 300 Franklin Street at the rear of Davies Symphony Hall. This event will feature a lucky draw and live music. The banquet will be catered by McCalls Catering & Events, with lighting design by Got Light. The décor for the event will feature hanging screens that highlight the many ways that Lunar New Year is celebrated across different cultures. Proceeds from the event support the Symphony’s artistic, education, and community programs. Tickets for the concert ($39- $109) and information about individual and full banquet table reservations can be found for purchase at sfsymphony.org, or through the box office at 415-864-6000. San Francisco Symphony’s Lunar New Year concert returns on Saturday, February 17.

articles.text: Certain topics used to be off-limits. Many of us learned to avoid controversial topics such as politics and religion. That was a very good policy. Let’s open the discussion with a very famous phrase which was uttered by one of the most controversial politicians ever. The phrase “Share the wealth” was used by Louisiana Governor Huey Long. Controversial he certainly was. The accusation of “demagogue” fits him very well. Now that I have your attention, let’s analyze how “share the wealth“ is a very good policy in the world of arts. Concert touring has changed greatly over the years. Not so many years ago, concert artists traveled from city to city by train. Let’s use this as a jumping off point and take it from there. A concert tour of the West Coast might start in Seattle, then continue to Portland. Next they would come to the Bay Area and play three concerts, one in San Francisco, another concert in Oakland, and a final concert in San Francisco. Then they’d play in San Jose, take the train to Santa Barbara, Los Angeles and finish in San Diego. Intercontinental plane travel put an end to this type of concert tour. We sometimes read of sister cities. Piedmont has a sister city, Cuneo, Italy, thanks for the efforts of Loretta Breuning and City Council member Jeff Wieler. I’ll bet only a few remember this connection. The last time I heard about Cuneo was when I was there in 2002 playing a concert. The mayor of Cuneo gave me a medal. The big-time concert artists have their own concert circuit. The others have to struggle for an existence. Perhaps, if we would work together, eve r yone cou ld benef it. The Piedmont Center for the Arts is our city’s gem. Quite obviously many of our citizens agree. The advice to share the wealth remains valuable, especially if you avoid the politics. articles.text: The singer and composer Danielle Wertz will be performing music from her newest album, Other Side, for two 7 p.m. and 8:30 p.m. shows on Friday, February 16 at SFJAZZ. “A masterful ballad interpreter” (NYC Jazz Record), the New York City-based vocalist and 2015 Thelonious Monk competition finalist weaves together elements of jazz, folk and her own voice used as an instrumental texture, to create an intimate musical world. A finalist in both the Ella Fitzgerald Jazz Vocal Competition and the Mid-Atlantic Jazz Vocal Competition, Wertz released her 2017 debut album Intertwined in collaboration with Israeli pianist Tal Cohen — a sparkling collection of standards and newer compositions which was ranked #4 on Capital Bop’s list of “Best DC Jazz Albums of 2017.” In addition to her solo career, Wertz is an avid collaborator, featured on recording projects alongside musicians Elena Pinderhughes, Braxton Cook, Justin Rock and Ambrose Akinmusire, among others. With Other Side, Wertz braves essential questions of the human experience with nuanced expression and deep feeling. Born of the introspection and examination that the pandemic forced upon us all, the album pairs her own lyrical compositions based in personal stories with carefully chosen covers like the Rogers and Hart classic “Spring is Here,” imbued with the longing and anger created by a world in lockdown. Tickets ($25) for the shows at SFJAZZ (201 Franklin St.) are available at sfjazz.org, or through the box office at 415-788-7353. articles.text: Viggo Mortensen and Kodi Smit-McPhee in The Road No doubt the world of Cormac McCarthy, author of the novel The Road, is bleak and austere. Recall his dark and nihilistic book, No Country for Old Men, also adapted to the screen by the Coen brothers. It won four Academy Awards, one for best picture. The Road is perhaps the most severe of all of McCarthy’s stories and director John Hillcoat follows the novel closely. The film is set during a post-apocalyptic period, one that has caused an ecological disaster, not unlike a nuclear winter. What happened is never made clear. The skies are leaden, a perpetual mist falls, all is grim and gray. A father (Viggo Mortensen) and his son (Kodi Smit-McPhee), ten years after the catalytic event, are on a road headed to the Pacific Ocean. Few people have survived the long torturous decade. Most have starved, been killed or committed suicide. The father and son are faced with overwhelming odds; they are desperate for food and constantly fearful of those they might meet along the way. The fragile patina of civilization has been scraped away, revealing the most sinister aspects of the human condition. They hide constantly from predators who will resort to anything to stay alive. Anything. All taboos have been broken. The intersection, between order and chaos, between laws and anarchy, intrigue McCarthy, and it’s an intersection that is explored in withering detail in The Road. The post-apocalyptic setting of this film is unrelentingly stark, with only a glimmer of hope embedded in this harsh, dystopian tale. The performances of Viggo Mortensen and Kodi SmitMcPhee are impressive. And with the exception of brief backstory, focusing on the mother (Charlize Theron), it is the father and son who make the journey, and it is their bond of love, their will to survive against all odds, that make for a compelling tale. Some might feel that The Road is too forbidding to be enjoyed. Yes, it is desolate; however, it is also far from the spectacle of most contemporary, apocalyptic blockbusters that assume that to hold filmgoers’ attention they must be overwhelmed by high volume drama, dazzled by seamless CGI, and taken for a harrowing ride. The Road is the antidote to such an assumption. The Road. Directed by John Hillcoat. Starring Viggo Mortensen, Kodi Smit-McPhee, Charlize Theron and Robert DuVall. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated R. Released 2009. Now streaming on VUDU/prime/apple tv.

articles.text: Max has all the right stuff to make it a winning movie for kids, say 10-years-old and up. It’s got a young teen boy, Justin (Josh Wiggins), feeling angry and rebellious, alienated from his strict ex-marine dad (Thomas Haden Church) and his kind mom (Lauren Graham). His brother, Kyle (Robbie Amell), is in Afghanistan where he and his squad are constantly on patrol for the bad guys. Along with Kyle goes Max, a trained military dog, wearing his own flak jacket, always scouting ahead, on the lookout for danger. Kyle is killed while on patrol and Max is sent back to the states to a small town in Texas. The dog (a Belgian Malinois) suffers from post-traumatic-stress as a result of the loss of Kyle and the ambush. As a result, his career over. Max is about to be put down. Justin and his mom and dad rescue Max, feeling he represents a tangible connection to their lost son, Kyle. Max, until he meets Justin, is, angry, snarling and lost. Eventually, they win each other over and team up. With the help of Justin’s friends, Chuy (Dejon La Quake) and Carmen (Mia Xitlai), a sweet love interest for Justin, they solve a Hardy Boys-type mystery involving some gangster types dealing in stolen guns and involving brother Kyle’s ex-marine buddy Tyler (Luke Kleintank), a stealthy villain. The last act has some intense action scenes where Justin and Max are both in harm’s way. As is Justin’s dad. The movie is sentimental and unabashedly schmaltzy. Indeed. In other words, it’s perfect summer fare for kids. Better than some the of big tent blockbusters. This is a straightforward boy and his dog movie, right out of the ‘50s. And it’s a perfect 4th of July movie (there is even a parade in act two). It also bears witness to the courage exemplified by what we refer to as “war dogs,” those canines that have a long and distinguished history, dating back to WWI. Be sure and stay for the credits. pages.text: Wednesday, February 7, 2024 21 MOVIE FOR KIDS Nanny McPhee Returns By Chris Honore’ Nanny McPhee was last seen in 2005, arriving to set right a dysfunctional family needing more than an intervention. They needed the McPhee magic, delivered by a snaggletooth, starched, ominous and mysterious nanny who arrives with magic at her fingertips and a cane to put things right. McPhee is a wonderful character, played perfectly by the gifted Emma Thompson. In the recent incarnation, Nanny McPhee Returns, written by Thompson, McPhee arrives at a bucolic farm in northern England. It’s the middle of WWII and children from London, which is subjected to Germany’s blitzkrieg bombing, are sent across England to wait out the war, most in the safety of the English countryside. And so we are introduced to the Green children and their mother, Isabel Green (Maggie Gyllenhaal). The family is hanging on by a thread, financially and emotionally, while waiting for the father to return from the war in Europe. What is a normal state of chaos on the farm turns chronic when cousins Cyril (Eros Vlahos) and Cella (Rosie Taylor-Ritson), arrive from upper crust London in a chauffer-driven limousine. Dressed to the nines, they refuse to step out of the car, holding their noses, insisting they’ve arrived at a “poo and mud” museum. Everything is icky, they want to go home, and dig in their snobbish custom made heels, refusing to help out. Things are dire. Isabel’s brothSee Nanny McPhee on page 32 Max – all about a dog in wartime By Chris Honoré Max has all the right stuff to make it a winning movie for kids, say 10-years-old and up. It’s got a young teen boy, Justin (Josh Wiggins), feeling angry and rebellious, alienated from his strict ex-marine dad (Thomas Haden Church) and his kind mom (Lauren Graham). His brother, Kyle (Robbie Amell), is in Afghanistan where he and his squad are constantly on patrol for the bad guys. Along with Kyle goes Max, a trained military dog, wearing his own flak jacket, always scouting ahead, on the lookout for danger. Kyle is killed while on patrol and Max is sent back to the states to a small town in Texas. The dog (a Belgian Malinois) suffers from post-traumatic-stress as a result of the loss of Kyle and the ambush. As a result, his career over. Max is about to be put down. Justin and his mom and dad rescue Max, feeling he represents a tangible connection to their lost son, Kyle. Max, until he meets Justin, is, angry, snarling and lost. Eventually, they win each other over and team up. With the help of Justin’s friends, Chuy (Dejon La Quake) and Carmen (Mia Xitlai), a sweet love interest for Justin, they solve a Hardy Boys-type mystery involving some gangster types dealing in stolen guns and involving brother Kyle’s ex-marine buddy Tyler (Luke Kleintank), a stealthy villain. The last act has some intense action scenes where Justin and Max are both in harm’s way. As is Justin’s dad. The movie is sentimental and unabashedly schmaltzy. Indeed. In other words, it’s perfect summer fare for kids. Better than some the of big tent blockbusters. This is a straightforward boy and his dog movie, right out of the ‘50s. And it’s a perfect 4th of July movie (there is even a parade in act two). It also bears witness to the courage exemplified by what we refer to as “war dogs,” those canines that have a long and distinguished history, dating back to WWI. Be sure and stay for the credits. In order to decide their order in the Chinese Zodiac cycle, the animals held a very exciting race. The first one to cross the river would be granted the first year, the second to come in would be the second animal in the cycle, and so on. The strong, hardworking Ox was in the lead. Suddenly, the clever Rat, jumped on the Ox’s back, he did not even feel the little thing getting a free ride. At the last second before reaching shore, the Rat jumped on land, winning the race! articles.text: You could see them coming from every direction, dozens of kids from K-5th grade and their families descending upon the Piedmont Community Church Gymnasium for the Annual Pinewood Derby. Races were held by age group every hour throughout the day. Piedmont BSA Cub Scouts held their competition in the morning, while the Girl Scouts of Northern California, Oakland Service Unit, held theirs in the afternoon. The Pinewood Derby is a Scouting tradition dating back to the 1950s. These days, the annual event is held by most packs around the country and works in the same way, regardless of location: Scouts race small, driverless wooden cars down a sloped track. The cars are powered only by gravity. With an adult’s help, each Pinewood Derby car is built by the child using a standard kit that includes a wooden block, plastic wheels, and metal axles. Prizes are awarded based on speed, design, and construction. Races started soon after check-in was complete. The competition was a double-elimination bracket, so each car raced twice to determine the event’s ultimate winners. Individual races typically lasted less than four seconds while the day’s especially fast cars usually clocked in at just over three. Winners in each category were provided with a certificate detailing their name and category. articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Coconut Mochi Cake is a traditional treat during Lunar New Year. February 10th marks the Lunar New Year of the Dragon. It is said that the lunar year harnesses the powers of its zodiac animal, so we are in for a favorable year as dragons symbolize strength and good fortune. A tradition in most Chinese families at Lunar New Year is nian gao (translation “Year Cake”), a steamed cake made of sweet rice flour and minimally processed cane sugar. We decorate it with sesame seeds and dried Chinese dates (jujubes) and steam it in a bed of bamboo leaves. This recipe is a twist, using coconut milk, granulated sugar, and baking the cake in a standard, 350°F oven. It’s an easier approach, especially if you do not regularly steam foods with a large steaming set-up. “Mochi cakes” have become very mainstream these days, with mochi as the sweet rice flour base in place of wheat flour. The cakes are adored for their soft and bouncy texture and are gluten-free. Coconut Mochi Cake – aka Chinese Nian Gao for Lunar New Year Adapted from What to Cook Today Makes one 8-inch round cake INGREDIENTS • 1/4 cup flaked coconut, unsweetened • 1-1/4 cup glutinous, sweet rice flour • 1 cup granulated sugar • 1/ 8 teaspoon salt • 2 extra-large eggs • 1-1/2 cups whole-fat coconut milk • 2 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted then cooled slightly; plus additional butter for the pan • 1/2 teaspoons coconut extract INSTRUCTIONS Toast the coconut flakes in a small, shallow pan over medium heat, stirring frequently, about five minutes until the edges of the flakes just begin to turn golden. Remove from the heat, transferring to a dish if needed to stop the browning. Set aside. Generously butter the sides of the cake pan and line the bottom with parchment paper. Position an oven rack one-third from the bottom of the oven. Preheat the oven to 350°F. Melt the 2 tablespoons of butter then transfer to a medium bowl. Add the 2 eggs and coconut extract then mix until combined. Add the coconut milk and mix again until well combined. (If the coconut milk as separated, warm it in a small saucepan over very low heat to re-emulsify. The coconut fat will melt at about 75°F – 80°F.) Mix the sweet rice flour, sugar, and salt together in a large bowl. Make a well in the center of the dry ingredients and add the liquid ingredients, stirring with a whisk to achieve a smooth, thin batter. Try to remove any lumps, straining if needed before pouring into the prepared pan. Bake for 30 minutes then remove from the oven and sprinkle on the reserved toasted coconut atop. Return to bake an additional 20 – 25 minutes until the cake is golden brown and the center is just barely set. A toothpick inserted into the center of the cake should come out with a few sticky bits, but not wet. Total baking time is about 50 – 55 minutes. Remove the cake from the oven and let cool for several hours before attempting to remove from the pan and cut. The cake is very soft and needs time to cool and set. Overnight in the refrigerator is also fine. For additional information and to search more recipes, see the blog of Piedmont resident Deborah Quok at: https://www. piedmontpantry.com/.

articles.text: Wednesday Walkers last week included Matt Gerhardt, Rick Eigenbrode, Mike Henn, Dottie Hutch, Christina Miller, Ken Hubbert, Maricela Negron, Mark Davis, Peggy Shultz, Will Adams, Marianne Jakus, Jim Kuo, Helen Dong, Lois Price, Rob Smith, Lori Austin, Martin Levy, Pat Keller, Elizabeth Richter, Sharona Fischrup, and Dick Carter. In 2023, the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group lived a charmed weather life. It never rained on Wednesday mornings. However in January, the threat of rain had to be part of their plans for weekly walks. Last Wednesda, rain was forecast for later in the day, so it was an opportunity for the group to live up to their “we walk rain or shine” mantra. Twenty-one walkers with umbrellas were at the Exedra Wednesday morning. A planned walking tour by architect Will Adams was postponed a week for better weather. The group went up Highland Avenue, turned up Oakland Avenue, and stopped in front of a house on the corner. This area was a bit of a Bohemian neighborhood in the early 20th Century. Writers and painters like Jack London and Xavier Martinez lived there in some unique homes. However, before them Frank C. Havens and his nephew, George Sterling, were residents in the area. His house was built in 1898 and might have been an early office for Havens, who was a local real estate developer in the late 19th and early 20th Centuries. He partnered with Francis “Borax” Smith, a businessman who made his fortune in borax mining, to create the Realty Syndicate in 1895, and they developed many of Oakland and Piedmont’s neighborhoods. Interestingly, both Havens and Sterling married their secretaries, and Sterling and his wife lived two houses up from this corner. The house at Highland and Oakland has a wonderful late 19th/early 20th Century look, with gables of different sizes and a witch cap roof in the front. Many of the homes in this neighborhood were built soon after the San Francisco Earthquake. After Piedmont became a city in 1907, home construction boomed. These streets were part of Wickham Havens’ (Frank’s son) Alta Piedmont Track and Alta Heights development. The walkers wondered if Havens’ “Alta Piedmont” resulted in the later references to “Baja Piedmont” for the streets below Highland. The group made a left turn on the one-block Hardwick Avenue and went up the Langdon Court cul-de-sac to enjoy their first cloudy view of San Francisco. The walkers returned to Hardwick, then on Blair and back to Highland to start the climb up Pala. They went on Mesa, enjoying more great homes built between 1906 to 1960, then it was up Pala to the Scenic-Pala steps where they climbed the 161-foot set of stairs. At the top, they went up Scenic for expansive views of the Bay and Mountain View Cemetery. An about-face took the walkers back down Scenic to more wonderful, cloudy San Francisco views and Blair Avenue. Going down Blair, the group quickly came to the house in which Jack London wrote his classic novel Call of the Wild. A closer look at the house found a fun, small street sign on a side gate that reads, “City of London Museum.” At this point, the walkers made their way directly down Blair to Highland and the Exedra before the sprinkles turned into the forecasted shower. It had been a fun, two-mile walk with wonderful homes, history, views, and friends on an only little-wet Wednesday morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.

His house was built in 1898 and might have been an early office for Havens, who was a local real estate developer in the late 19th and early 20th Centuries. He partnered with Francis “Borax” Smith, a businessman who made his fortune in borax mining, to create the Realty Syndicate in 1895, and they developed many of Oakland and Piedmont’s neighborhoods. Interestingly, both Havens and Sterling married their secretaries, and Sterling and his wife lived two houses up from this corner. The house at Highland and Oakland has a wonderful late 19th/early 20th Century look, with gables of different sizes and a witch cap roof in the front. Many of the homes in this neighborhood were built soon after the San Francisco Earthquake. After Piedmont became a city in 1907, home construction boomed. These streets were part of Wickham Havens’ (Frank’s son) Alta Piedmont Track and Alta Heights development. The walkers wondered if Havens’ “Alta Piedmont” resulted in the later references to “Baja Piedmont” for the streets below Highland. The group made a left turn on the one-block Hardwick Avenue and went up the Langdon Court cul-de-sac to enjoy their first cloudy view of San Francisco. The walkers returned to Hardwick, then on Blair and back to Highland to start the climb up Pala. They went on Mesa, enjoying more great homes built between 1906 to 1960, then it was up Pala to the Scenic-Pala steps where they climbed the 161-foot set of stairs. At the top, they went up Scenic for expansive views of the Bay and Mountain View Cemetery. An about-face took the walkers back down Scenic to more wonderful, cloudy San Francisco views and Blair Avenue. Going down Blair, the group quickly came to the house in which Jack London wrote his classic novel Call of the Wild. A closer look at the house found a fun, small street sign on a side gate that reads, “City of London Museum.” At this point, the walkers made their way directly down Blair to Highland and the Exedra before the sprinkles turned into the forecasted shower. It had been a fun, two-mile walk with wonderful homes, history, views, and friends on an only little-wet Wednesday morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.
